title: Far-off sangats
hookLine: early sangats grew in Kabul, Dhaka and Patna, sending offerings and receiving letters

cards: Anandpur, and a caravan coming in from the northwest, over the mountain passes, dusty and tired. Tradition says it's the sangat of Kabul, bringing gifts for the Guru, among them a fine canopy.

They've traveled a very long way to stand in his presence for a little while. Then they'll turn around and make the whole journey again, home to a city where the Guru may never set foot. Today: far-off sangats.

teach.b: Sangat means the company, the gathered community. A listener might assume the Sikhs of the Gurus' time all lived around Punjab, within a few days' walk. Tradition tells a wider story.
Guru Nanak traveled far, and where he went, people remembered. Later Gurus traveled too.
Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur journeyed east through Patna and on to Dhaka and Assam, and sangats in those places kept his memory and their gatherings going after he left.
Sikhs remember Patna, on the Ganges, as the place where Guru Gobind Singh was born and spent his early childhood, cared for by the sangat there. To the northwest, there was Kabul.
So how did a sangat a long journey away stay close to a Guru it might never see? Three ways run through the stories.
First, they gave. Far-off Sikhs sent offerings, a share of their earnings, carried by travelers and representatives to the Guru's court.
Second, they came. Some, like the Kabul sangat, made the long trip themselves when they could.
Third, they listened. Letters went out from the Guru to these sangats, read aloud when they gathered. That's tomorrow's story, so we'll leave the letters sealed for now.

Distance didn't make these Sikhs second-class. In the tellings, their gatherings are sangats in full: singing the Gurus' hymns, keeping their own kitchens, and sending their love across mountains and rivers.
A sangat, in this story, isn't measured by how close it sits to the center. It's measured by whether it keeps gathering.

how: Sikhs honor Takht Sri Patna Sahib as Guru Gobind Singh's birthplace, and gurdwaras in places the Gurus visited keep the memory of the early sangats that gathered there.

practice: Bring to mind someone who matters to you and lives far away. Picture where they are right now, what time it is there, what their room might look like, and notice that the distance hasn't erased them from you.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Far-off sangats. The Sikh gatherings in places like Kabul, Dhaka and Patna that stayed close to the Gurus by giving, coming and listening. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the company, the gathered community.

carryVoice: Your line: far off, still close. Mountains between, and still one sangat. Day eight hundred thirty-four, done.
